cells.tense: You are keeping something alive in other people, and you are doing it now.
cells.ask: Tell one person today why a practice of yours still matters, not just how to do it. Then let their version of it come out different from yours.
cells.core:
You are carrying something forward and handing it to people in a way they can pick up and use. It doesn't arrive as an order, and it doesn't arrive as a lecture — it lands because you keep adjusting it to the person in front of you. That is the whole trick, and it is working.

You can feel which part of it is still worth keeping and which part has gone stiff, and you hold both at once: what came down to you and the person in front of you. That is not an easy balance. Most of it happens quietly and you won't usually get told you did it right. Say out loud why a piece of it matters, and the next person carries it forward as their own instead of just copying the shape.
cells.sheetLine: You carry the old thing in a way a new person can hold.
cells.verb: carrying meaning forward and keeping it alive in other people
cells.place: standing where the going keeps its hold on you

cells.tense: You are pressing a future onto people that has not arrived and may never ask to be written in.
cells.ask: For one conversation, drop the lesson and just do the thing with someone — make it, cook it, sing it. Say nothing about why it matters.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead of you is a version where people have it right, and you are working backward from it. Each talk turns into a chance to get them there. The rules get firmer as you go, and the door you are trying to hold open gets narrower.

What you are protecting is real. What is slipping is the thing itself — the letter stays and the liveliness goes. Nobody gets argued into meaning something. When you insist on the shape, people comply or they leave, and either way the thing you were carrying stops moving through them. It stops being handed on and starts being enforced. The grip is what's costing you, not the meaning.
cells.sheetLine: The version you're forcing on people isn't the one they can hold.
cells.verb: carrying meaning forward and keeping it alive in other people

cells.tense: You were left sorting this out alone, and you are still doing it alone in ways you may not notice.
cells.ask: Write one thought down the plain way, no made-up words, and send it to one person who'd get it. Just that.
cells.core:
Nothing got handed to you that you fully trust, so when you need a frame you build one from scratch. You are good at it. You are also doing it in a room by yourself, over and over.

There's a pattern under how all this works, and you of all people can see it. That's the way back — not more feeling, not more effort into chasing things you're not sure you want. Look at the machinery clearly and the pull toward something returns on its own. When you find the shape of something, you stop needing to invent it alone. What you build can be handed to someone else and it holds. You won't have to rebuild the same thing again next year.
cells.sheetLine: You keep building it alone because nothing was passed down clean.

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy from, and you talk about it as if it were happening without you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you do that someone has picked up from you, and say plainly that you're the one who does it.
cells.core:
People are taking things from you. A word you use, how you handle a mess, the way you stay calm when something goes wrong — it goes into them and comes back out of their mouths. You describe that as just how things are around here.

You're the source of it. That's not a promotion, it's a plain fact you haven't said out loud yet. Calling it yours changes what you do with it, because then you can adjust it instead of letting it run ungrounded. There's an easier, earlier version of this that's still available — the way you did it before it got complicated. Saying it's yours brings that back within reach.
cells.sheetLine: People take their cue from you, and you call it nothing.

attempts.check: The record does not license saying this person has a specific lineage, faith, or family they have broken from, so Too Little must stay on the mechanism of rebuilding a shared frame without naming or dating any loss. A reader could reasonably say their loneliness of thought is chosen solitude rather than a gap, and the ask still works either way because writing one thought plainly to one person is an act, not a confession that they lack anything. The line that would serve me more than them is 'every generation reinventing the wheel' — it flatters the reader by making their isolation sound like a distinction, so I've dropped it from the cell entirely.
